ap_biology-m01.set_intro: A biologist samples a population of a plant species and records the genotypes at a gene with two alleles, A and a. The table shows the data.

stimulus.description: Genotypes of 1000 individuals in a population sampled at one time

items.stem: What is the frequency of allele a in the population?

options.why: Counts the proportion of homozygous recessive individuals instead of the allele frequency.
Reports the frequency of the dominant allele.
There are 2000 alleles. The number of a alleles is 286 + 2(257) = 800, so the frequency of a is 800/2000 = 0.40.
Divides the number of a alleles by the number of individuals instead of the number of alleles.

blueprint.subject: ap_biology
student_thinking: Identify the biological principle or relationship that governs the situation: allele frequency from genotype counts
Apply it to the information given and compare the result with the four options

key_conditions.condition: every quantity or fact needed is given in the stem or the stimulus

misconceptions.description: Counts the proportion of homozygous recessive individuals instead of the allele frequency.
Reports the frequency of the dominant allele.
Divides the number of a alleles by the number of individuals instead of the number of alleles.

verification.independent_path: allele counting vs the generating q

blueprint.judgment_demand: choose the governing biological relationship, then apply or interpret it

items.stem: If the population were in Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium with the allele frequencies found in the previous question, how many heterozygotes would be expected?

options.why: Uses p times q times the population size, without the factor of 2.
Applying the relationship to the values given in the question and the stimulus gives 480; each other option comes from a specific, named error.
Uses 2pq as a number without multiplying by the population size.
Uses p squared times the population size.

Apply it to the information given and compare the result with the four options

key_conditions.condition: every quantity or fact needed is given in the stem or the stimulus

misconceptions.description: Uses p times q times the population size, without the factor of 2.
Uses 2pq as a number without multiplying by the population size.
Uses p squared times the population size.

items.stem: Which statement best compares the observed number of heterozygotes with the expected number?

options.text: The population has about the expected number of heterozygotes, so it is in Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium.
options.why: The observed number differs a lot from the expected number.

options.text: The population has more heterozygotes than expected (286 observed and about 480 expected), so it is not in equilibrium.
options.why: The observed number of heterozygotes is lower than expected, not higher.

options.text: The population has fewer heterozygotes than expected (286 observed and about 480 expected), so it is not in Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium.
options.why: A large deficit of heterozygotes is not consistent with the equilibrium genotype frequencies.

options.text: The comparison cannot be made, because Hardy-Weinberg applies only to dominant alleles.
options.why: Hardy-Weinberg applies to alleles of a gene in a population.

verification.independent_path: observed minus expected heterozygotes vs the generating inbreeding

items.stem: Which condition of Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium is most likely to have been violated?

options.text: A very large population, which prevents chance changes in allele frequencies
options.why: A large population helps maintain equilibrium and would not cause a heterozygote deficit.

options.text: Nonrandom mating, such as mating between relatives, which increases the proportion of homozygotes
options.why: Inbreeding raises the frequency of homozygotes and lowers the frequency of heterozygotes without changing allele frequencies.

options.text: Random mating among all the individuals in the population
options.why: Random mating is a condition for equilibrium, not a violation.

options.text: No mutation, because the alleles are not changed
options.why: The absence of mutation would help keep equilibrium.
